summary: Deep dive on integrating OpenTelemetry for token-level metrics and traces. Covered span design (model.call, token.emit), attributes to capture (model, variant, batch.size, kv.cache.hit), metrics (per-token latency p50/p95, tokens/sec), and dashboard patterns. Discussed on-prem/VPC OTLP collector flow, privacy/anonymization, costs of high-cardinality tags, and tradeoffs for batching and KV cache instrumentation.
topics: Span design and tags for model calls
Batching visibility and per-batch vs per-token metrics
Quantization impact on latency and instrumentation
VPC / on-prem OTEL flow and egress considerations
transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-11-18 15:30 UTC | Duration: 62 minutes
Attendees: Ari Chen, Samira Patel, Diego Morales (Redwood) / Janelle Ruiz, Mark Li, Kevin O'Neal (CortexAI)

[00:00] Ari (Redwood): hey everyone thanks for joining, we're going to do a technical deep dive on observability and stitching redwood into OTEL. quick agenda — tracing, token metrics, dashboards, and on-prem considerations. sound good?
[00:12] Janelle (CortexAI): yep sounds perfect, we mainly want token-level visibility and to understand kv cache behavior, plus anything that affects our SLOs.
[00:20] Samira (Redwood SE): cool, i'll start with the span model we recommend. high level: each model ingestion is a root span (model.call) with child spans for decoder steps/token emissions if you want per-token tracing. we usually do per-request spans and emit per-token metrics rather than creating thousands of spans, because span cardinality and cost can blow up — but for debugging you can enable token spans.
[00:45] Mark (CortexAI): when you say token metrics, do you mean per-token latency metrics? that's potentially a lot, how do you roll up?
[00:53] Samira: good q. we capture a metric tokens.emitted with labels: model.name, model.variant, batch.size, producer (host or client), and kv_cache_hit boolean. then we emit latency histograms: token.latency_ms with p50, p95 buckets aggregated in OTLP. we recommend aggregation at collector to reduce ingestion.
[01:15] Diego (Redwood SRE): also important — we tag spans with sequence_id and request_id but avoid user prompt text. privacy. we advise hashing prompt ids if you need correlation.
[01:28] Kevin (CTO): we run in a locked-down VPC and can't talk to external collectors, how would OTLP work?
[01:34] Ari: two options: 1) deploy an OTLP collector inside your VPC that forwards to Redwood's ingest over a peered private line (or S3/HSM bucket sync), or 2) push to your internal observability stack (Prometheus + Grafana + Jaeger) and share dashboards or allow Redwood read-only access. For on-prem you can run the same collectors and ship periodically.
[01:55] Janelle: any latency overhead from emitting token metrics? I'm worried about the per-token serialization cost.
[02:01] Samira: negligible if you batch metrics and use non-blocking exporters. The runtime is instrumented with async buffers; token counters are incremented in memory and flushed every second. The expensive piece is high-cardinality labels — e.g., including user_id or prompt hash per-token will spike cardinality.
[02:20] [02:20] Mark: what about KV cache metrics? we want to see cache hit-rate per model variant and per key TTL distribution.
[02:27] Samira: we expose metrics: kv.cache.hits, kv.cache.misses, kv.cache.size_bytes, kv.cache.evictions, and kv.cache.latency_ms. each of those can be labeled by model.variant, shard_id, and cache_tier (local vs remote). we also emit a sampled trace on cache miss that includes the upstream fetch span so you can see the end-to-end penalty.
[02:48] Diego: note — sample the cache-miss traces at 1-5% by default. otherwise traces could be enormous.
[02:55] Janelle: in your examples do you show how batching affects token latency breakdown? our workloads have lots of short prompts and some long ones — we need per-batch stats.
[03:06] Samira: yes. we emit batch.metrics: batch.size_counts, batch.latency_ms, per-batch token_count. Then we also emit derived per-token latency by dividing batch.latency by token_count for rough estimates; but for accurate per-token we rely on token.emit metrics as i said. The dashboards should show both distribution and heatmaps: batch size distribution vs p95 latency.
[03:30] Mark: is quantization visible in the metrics? e.g., quantized models run faster but maybe higher variance.
[03:37] Samira: model.variant label includes quantization profile, e.g., gptq-4bit or fp16. So you can slice p50/p95 by variant. We also emit executor.metrics like kernel.exec_time_ms and memory.pressure to help correlate regressions.
[03:52] Kevin: curious about storage of these token-level metrics long-term. storing per-token for weeks is expensive.
[03:58] Ari: we recommend short retention for high-cardinality raw metrics (7-14 days) and rollups for long-term (monthly aggregates). Redwood's Optimize product can do intelligent rollups and keep sample-based archives for regression detection.
[04:15] Janelle: ok, show me a quick example of an OTEL snippet — how to instrument a python client or runtime hook.
[04:22] Samira: sure i'll read a short snippet — this is approximate, transcription may be rough:
[04:28] Samira: "from opentelemetry import metrics, trace
tracer = trace.get_tracer('redwood-runtime')
with tracer.start_as_current_span('model.call', attributes={'model.name':'gpt-3-og', 'model.variant':'gptq-4bit'}):
  # when token emitted
  token_counter.add(1, {'kv_cache_hit':'true','batch.size':batch_size})
  latency_hist.record(token_latency_ms, {'model.variant':variant})"
[04:55] Mark: so you add labels per call, if we push these to our collector we should be able to render in grafana?
[05:00] Samira: yep. exporter -> OTLP -> Prometheus remote_write or direct OTLP to your Metrics backend. For traces we suggest Jaeger or Tempo, and you can stitch traces to metrics via request_id.
[05:12] Kevin: any gotchas for VPC egress?
[05:15] Diego: yes, allowlisting endpoints and using mutual TLS or VPC peering is common. some customers prefer an on-prem collector that does local aggregation and only ships compressed rollups to Redwood. also consider OTLP grpc vs http protocols; grpc is more efficient.
[05:32] Janelle: about privacy — we can't include prompt text. does Redwood need the prompt at all to correlate?
[05:37] Ari: no. correlation is via request_id and hashed prompt ids. Redwood never needs raw prompt content for observability; for evaluation or quality checks you'd send guarded samples with consent.
[05:48] Mark: what's the recommended sampling rate for token spans vs request spans?
[05:52] Samira: default: sample 100% of request-level spans. Token-level spans sample 1-5% or enabled only for canary clusters. Cache-miss traces maybe sampled at higher rate because they're informative.
[06:05] Kevin: on the dashboard side, what templates do you provide?
[06:09] Samira: we have Grafana templates: model overview (QPS, tokens/s, p50/p95 token latency), cache dashboard (hit-rate, evictions, TTL distribution), batch dashboard (heatmap of batch sizes vs p95), and a trace panel linking to Jaeger. we'll share links.
[06:22] Janelle: can you demo a sample dashboard real quick?
[06:25] Samira: i don't have the live one in this call but i can share screenshots and a JSON export after. typical panels include token.latency_ms p50/p95 by variant, tokens.emitted rate, and kv.cache.hit_rate as a derived ratio.
[06:40] Ari: practical note — avoid high-cardinality labels like user_id or conversation_id on metrics. Use them on traces only and sample.
[06:47] Mark: what about cost impact — we have tight budget for observability ingress.
[06:51] Diego: tradeoffs: reduce label set, sample traces, aggregate at collector, and use histograms with limited buckets. Redwood can recommend specific metrics to keep at high fidelity and which to roll up.
[07:06] Janelle: what about instrumentation for quantization regressions? we want alerts when throughput drops after a q4 rollout.
[07:12] Samira: use comparative dashboards: compare model.variant:q4 vs variant:fp16 over rolling windows. set alert on regression delta for p95 token latency or tokens/sec. Also tie alerts to a canary group so you auto-failback.
[07:28] Kevin: ok, on the implementation plan, we need: example OTEL config, an internal collector layout for VPC, recommended labels, dashboards, and a short benchmark with our sample traffic.
[07:37] Ari: that's exactly what we'll deliver. Samira will share the OTEL snippets and Grafana json, Diego will confirm allowlist and network approach, and Mark will send sample traffic.
[07:48] Janelle: timeline? can we get the OTEL snippets by friday?
[07:50] Samira: yes i'll send by 2026-11-20.
[07:55] Kevin: last Q — does Redwood store any raw metrics that include prompt content in hosted mode?
[07:59] Ari: no, by default no prompt contents. We store aggregated metrics and traces with attributes; any raw prompt materials are opt-in. We'll include that in the security doc.
[08:10] Mark: great, thanks.
[08:12] Ari: thanks all. recap of next steps — see action items. we'll follow up with schedule for benchmark next week.

[End of transcript]
